case_study_insert.main_stem: Hallam & Grey Electrical (HGE) is a private limited company in the consumer electronics and home appliance retail sector, employing a workforce of 132 across nine superstores in the Norwick region and an online shop. Founded in 2009 by Nadia Rahman, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. HGE plans to invest $980,000 in a next-day home-delivery fulfilment centre with an in-house repair workshop, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $500,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $55, and currently produces 32,000 units a year. HGE faces a growing operational problem: labour turnover among shop-floor sales staff has climbed sharply, and customer complaints about late deliveries are increasing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary (October 2026): A survey of 800 customers across the nine superstores found that 58% would switch to HGE for a price-match guarantee, 71% check online reviews before buying appliances, and 46% said free next-day delivery would decide where they buy. The online shop processed 9,600 orders last quarter with a return rate of 3.1%. In-store repair counters completed 640 jobs with a 6.2% rework rate. Average delivery time is 2.4 days. Monthly customer complaints fell from 52 to 34 after the staff service scheme began. Of the 132 employees, 38 work as shop-floor sales staff; off-the-job training at the Norwick regional college costs $1,100 per employee, while on-the-job training is delivered in the superstores.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Hallam & Grey Electrical as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing repayments for retailers with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $11.80 to $12.64 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid retail staff. (3) Consumer electronics prices fell 3.6% year-on-year as global supply eased, inflation is running at 3.4%, and household spending on electrical goods grew 2.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HGE plans to finance its $980,000 home-delivery fulfilment centre with a $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HGE of using retained profit rather than borrowing the full amount.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $380,000 of its own retained profit costs HGE nothing in repayments or interest, which eases cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $500,000 a year and is about to service a $600,000 ten-year loan. The retained-profit route also protects HGE from interest-rate risk: the central bank has just raised the base rate to 5.0%, so each further 0.25% rise would add $1,500 a year to a variable-rate $600,000 loan (0.0025 x $600,000), and retained profit avoids that exposure entirely for this portion of the funding.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps decision-making with Nadia Rahman and HGE's directors, with no lender covenants dictating how the fulfilment centre, delivery schedule or pricing are run. It also signals financial strength to suppliers, helping HGE negotiate better terms as it scales the nine superstores plus the online shop, which processed 9,600 orders last quarter, into next-day fulfilment. Using internal funds also avoids security being pledged against the new $980,000 centre, keeping the expansion fully under HGE's control while labour turnover among shop-floor staff is being fixed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hallam & Grey Electrical and its fulfilment centre expansion.

questions.question_text: HGE is launching its next-day home-delivery service. Consider a national television advertising campaign, a regional newspaper advertising campaign, or social media advertising. Which should HGE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A national TV campaign would give the launch huge reach very quickly and could put HGE's next-day delivery promise in front of millions of viewers across the country. However, production and airtime costs for national slots are extremely high for a nine-superstore regional retailer, and a large share of the audience would live far beyond the Norwick region HGE actually serves. With complaints about late deliveries still fresh and labour turnover climbing, tying up capital in wasteful national coverage is hard to justify when the expansion already absorbs $980,000.

Regional newspaper campaign: Local and regional newspapers are far cheaper than national television and reach the Norwick catchment where HGE's nine superstores and online customers are concentrated. Newspaper advertising suits price-led, time-bound messages such as launch offers. Its weaknesses are a shrinking and older readership, limited space for visual demonstrations of the new fulfilment promise, and poor measurability compared with digital channels, given that 71% of HGE customers check online reviews before buying.

Social media advertising: Social campaigns let HGE target its exact 46% of surveyed shoppers who said free next-day delivery would decide where they buy, plus the 71% who research online. Spend is measurable click by click, creative can be adjusted quickly, and it keeps the cost far below television. Reach among younger appliance buyers is strong, though it demands consistent content production and some spend on paid promotion to stand out.

Recommendation: HGE should choose social media advertising. It is the cheapest of the three per relevant customer reached, it is measurable, and it targets precisely the online-review-checking segment identified in HGE's own research, reinforcing the 9,600-order online channel. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional nine-superstore chain funding an $980,000 expansion from retained profit and a $600,000 loan; the regional newspaper is rejected as too narrow in reach and weak for younger buyers. Social media should be supported by in-store posters, but it should carry the launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HGE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HGE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the regional newspaper are rejected.

questions.question_text: HGE faces rising labour turnover among its shop-floor sales staff. Explain two benefits for HGE of democratic leadership in its superstores.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HGE's 38 shop-floor sales staff a real voice in rota design, service standards and how the repair counters are run, which raises job satisfaction and morale. Staff who feel consulted are less likely to leave, directly attacking the labour turnover problem identified in the case. Higher engagement also improves service attitude, helping to push the monthly complaint count back down toward the 34 achieved after the staff service scheme began.

Point 2: Involving staff surfaces front-line ideas that managers at head office cannot see, for example which appliance models generate the 6.2% rework rate on repair counters and how delivery slots could be sequenced to cut late drop-offs. Better decisions reduce complaints and protect the online promise of 2.4-day delivery. Because HGE already operates democratic leadership within a hierarchical structure, extending consultation is a low-cost change: it improves retention, protects the service levels that justify next-day delivery, and reduces the $1,100 per employee off-the-job retraining spend and the disruption of constantly recruiting replacements for the 132-strong workforce.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HGE's labour turnover, rework rate and service levels.

questions.question_text: HGE must retrain staff for the new fulfilment centre and in-house repair workshop. Consider on-the-job training in the superstores or off-the-job training at the Norwick regional college. Which should HGE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training staff in the superstores and repair counters is machine- and process-specific, costs nothing in fees, and keeps employees productive while they learn, which is vital when the online shop must maintain its 2.4-day delivery promise across 9,600 orders a quarter. It also allows repair procedures that currently produce a 6.2% rework rate to be corrected in context. Drawbacks are that experienced staff time is diverted from customers, bad habits can be copied, and formal certification is limited, which could matter if the new repair workshop wants to market its credentials.

Off-the-job training: The Norwick regional college course at $1,100 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate, which would help HGE market the repair workshop's credibility to sceptical customers. If all 38 shop-floor sales staff attended, the bill would be $41,800 (38 x $1,100), on top of covering their absence from the superstores. College content is generic, however, and may not match HGE's exact equipment and stock systems, so follow-up coaching would still be required; the insert does not state how many staff actually need the workshop training, so this $41,800 is an upper bound, not a forecast.

Decision: HGE should choose on-the-job training as the core route, reserving college places for a small number of lead technicians. It is cheaper, immediate, specific to the repair workshop's equipment, and avoids removing sales staff from the floor during a launch already straining service levels. Full off-the-job training for all 38 staff is rejected because $41,800 plus lost floor cover would strain the $500,000 fixed-cost base, and generic courses would still need in-store reinforcement; a blended approach captures the certificate benefit without the full cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HGE.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HGE with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the repair workshop.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HGE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $500,000 / ($55 - $30) = $500,000 / $25 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Current output - Break-even output. Substitution: 32,000 units - 20,000 units = 12,000 units. Answer: the margin of safety is 12,000 units.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HGE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HGE's managers can compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 32,000 units to confirm the superstores comfortably clear fixed costs, with a margin of safety of 12,000 units, before scaling the fulfilment centre to next-day volumes.
2. The $25 contribution per unit lets managers model promotional pricing; a 10% launch discount would cut the selling price to $49.50 and contribution to $19.50, so managers can judge whether the extra volume still covers the $500,000 fixed costs of the expanded operation.
3. Knowing break-even output helps managers stress-test the $600,000 bank loan: if online and superstore demand fell below 20,000 units a year, fixed costs of $500,000 a year would not be recovered, signalling the need to control costs or renegotiate supplier terms.
4. Managers can use labour productivity data (32,000 units / 132 employees = 242.4 units per employee) to set performance targets, identify understaffed superstores, and decide how many of the 38 shop-floor staff can be redeployed to the repair workshop without service levels slipping.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 12,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: output headroom vs the 32,000-unit volume; discount modelling against the $25 contribution and $500,000 fixed costs; loan stress-testing at the 20,000-unit break-even point; and labour productivity of 242.4 units per employee to plan staffing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HGE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HGE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.44 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.80 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $480,000 inventories + $265,000 trade receivables + $150,000 cash = $895,000; 2025 current assets = $520,000 + $310,000 + $210,000 = $1,040,000. Ratio 2024 = $895,000 / $620,000 = 1.44; 2025 = $1,040,000 / $650,000 = 1.60. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($895,000 - $480,000) / $620,000 = $415,000 / $620,000 = 0.67; 2025 = ($1,040,000 - $520,000) / $650,000 = $520,000 / $650,000 = 0.80.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities improved from 1.44 to 1.60, and the quick measure that excludes inventories improved from 0.67 to 0.80, helped by cash rising from $150,000 to $210,000 and current liabilities growing only from $620,000 to $650,000 while assets grew faster. Trade receivables climbed from $265,000 to $310,000, which matters for HGE because superstore and repair-counter sales to trade customers on account could stretch the very cash buffer funding the $980,000 fulfilment centre. Inventories also grew from $480,000 to $520,000 ahead of the launch, which will convert back into cash only if the 9,600-order pipeline is fulfilled without repeat of the late-delivery complaints.

Conclusion: HGE's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.44 to 1.60) and the acid test ratio (0.67 to 0.80) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement is not an illusion created by warehouse stock. HGE should still tighten trade-customer credit control and monitor delivery performance before committing further capital, but the trend supports the $980,000 expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HGE's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HGE of offering free next-day delivery on online appliance orders.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free next-day delivery directly targets the 46% of surveyed shoppers who said it would decide where they buy appliances, and it differentiates HGE from rivals given that 71% of customers check online reviews before purchasing. It leverages the 9,600 orders processed last quarter, nudging more research-stage browsers into buying, and it strengthens loyalty as shoppers come to expect the promise. Because it applies only online, it also steers higher-margin, delivery-friendly sales toward the fulfilment centre now being built, supporting the $980,000 investment case.

Disadvantage: Offering it free means HGE absorbs the cost gap between the current 2.4-day service and a next-day network itself, and if the fulfilment centre is late, the exact complaint HGE is trying to fix becomes a public liability that damages trust and margin. Free delivery can also pull basket size down if shoppers buy single low-value accessories, while packaging, driver and warehouse costs will sit inside the $500,000 fixed-cost base before throughput reaches target volumes. HGE must price the promise into margins or set a minimum order value, or the scheme erodes the contribution it depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HGE's research data, delivery promise and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 3.6% fall in electronics prices will affect HGE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If HGE's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the full 0.75% rise adds 0.0075 x $600,000 = $4,500 a year to repayments; on top of that, each 0.25% step is $1,500 a year. That is under 1% of HGE's $500,000 fixed-cost base and is manageable, though it raises the hurdle rate for any further borrowing for the $980,000 fulfilment centre. If the loan was fixed at the outset, the cash impact today is zero, but higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about big-ticket appliance purchases and would raise the cost of any future variable-rate borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $12.64 per hour): HGE has a workforce of 132 and 38 shop-floor sales staff are hourly-paid, so this rise is unavoidable and applies to every hour they work. The insert gives no wage rates or hours, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the correct lens is productivity, 32,000 units / 132 employees = 242.4 units per employee. The wage rise is affordable only if this productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $30 variable cost per unit effectively increases, squeezing HGE's contribution per unit.

Fall in electronics prices (3.6% year-on-year): Lower prices reduce what HGE pays for stock, easing pressure on the $30 variable cost and margins. The same deflation, however, drags on the $55 selling price, so headline revenue per unit may fall even if volume grows; 2.2% growth in household spending on electrical goods against 3.4% inflation may mask weak real demand, and HGE cannot count on price increases to recover wage or delivery costs.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is certain, recurring and touches all 38 hourly-paid shop-floor staff directly, whereas the interest rise is at most $4,500 a year and could be zero if the loan is fixed, and falling electronics prices cut HGE's input costs as well as its selling prices, so they are partly self-offsetting. HGE should protect its contribution by lifting productivity through the rework fix rather than raising prices into a deflating market.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HGE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HGE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HGE with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
